title: Please review the research in /papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/02_spatial_tensor_zero_spacings. Which tensor network seems to work better, the one that outputs the gaps or the one that outputs the zeros?

parts: Please review the research in /papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/02_spatial_tensor_zero_spacings. Which tensor network seems to work better, the one that outputs the gaps or the one that outputs the zeros?
I’ll read the investigation’s comparisons and check how each network performed on zero locations, neighboring gaps, and held-out data.

The two versions use the same spatial tree. The position study withheld the final zero locations and predicted both from their initial positions and velocities. The gap study answered a different question: it identified a neighboring zero that explains why the spacing bends upward. I’ll check the recorded bounds against the direct calculations.

**I’d choose the version that outputs the zeros for prediction, and keep the gap output for explaining why the spacing changes.** Both use the same spatial tree. On the tested pair near Newman heights 28 and 42, both zeros moved toward smaller heights, by about \(5.80\times10^{-5}\) and \(7.55\times10^{-5}\). Their positions capture that shared motion. The gap records only the difference, a shrinkage of about \(1.75\times10^{-5}\). [Position results](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/02_spatial_tensor_zero_spacings/notes/13_AGC_ST_Z_POSITION_MILESTONE_AND_CONTINUATION_20261120.md:10)

With the final locations withheld, the zero-output version used the initial positions and velocities, a fixed exterior probe, and certified counts and signs to predict both locations at \(t=10^{-4}\). Its interval widths were below \(1.574\times10^{-10}\) and \(8.466\times10^{-11}\). Direct bisection of the same field gave tighter brackets, \(2^{-54}\) per zero. Whether the tree saves work at comparable accuracy across many zeros remains open. [Comparison and replay](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/02_spatial_tensor_zero_spacings/reviews/06_AGC_ST_GAP_AND_POSITION_COMPARISON_20261120.md:9)

The **gap output** gave the clearer explanation of curvature. It showed that one exterior zero near height 50 contributes enough to prove \(g''>1/180\) throughout the interval. The gap was shrinking, and its shrinkage was slowing. Simply subtracting the two acceleration intervals from the fixed-probe position forecast leaves both signs possible. [Gap proof](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/02_spatial_tensor_zero_spacings/notes/06_AGC_ST_E06_FINITE_GAP_CURVATURE_20261120.md:30)

Can you modify the second research overview, plan and progress files with this perspective? Also, please make the research program focus primarily on analytical frameworks that can lead to simplifications which could ideally lead to control over the gap chain dynamics and moments being studied in 05_arithmetic_gap_continuation. First focus on finding the natural equations that determine how the tensor network is set up and how it evolves in time, before specializing to any specific system or test cases.

I’ll revise the three position-program files so the first research question is what determines the tree and its time evolution. I’ll check how the parent investigation defines the gap chain and its moments, and preserve the completed position and gap results as evidence for the revised plan.

The branch already has an exact rule for combining neighboring blocks and a heat-flow equation for each block. I’ll make the next task build on those results: determine which information a block must exchange to evolve in time, then ask whether sharing that information across adjacent gaps simplifies the parent moment equations. The proposed two-probe experiment will move behind that work.

The revised plan now asks whether a smaller set of variables can evolve from the information retained at each cut. It also names the standard for a useful simplification: a bound that reaches an individual gap or moment after neighboring blocks are combined. I’m checking that the progress register and older continuation links point to that sequence.

I revised the second overview, plan, and progress register. **The program now starts by deriving what each spatial block must store, what information crosses a cut, and how those quantities evolve in time.** The equations must give the same result whether two blocks evolve separately and then combine, or combine first and evolve together. Individual zeros remain the preferred prediction. Gaps and exterior moments explain their relative motion. [Research overview](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/02_spatial_tensor_zero_spacings/research-overview/02_AGC_ST_ZERO_POSITIONS_RESEARCH_OVERVIEW_20261120.md:7)

The plan then asks whether adjacent gaps can share a smaller set of exterior quantities. A useful simplification would eliminate an independent unknown from a parent moment equation or bound how much the omitted terms can change an individual gap over time. The next step would track whether that control survives as more edges are joined. [Research plan](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/02_spatial_tensor_zero_spacings/research-plan/02_AGC_ST_ZERO_POSITIONS_RESEARCH_PLAN_20261120.md:19)

**AGC-ST-Z-B06 is the next task.** It begins with symbolic blocks and a general field evolution. I deferred the two-probe experiment near heights 42 and 50 until the analysis identifies a specific question it could settle, and updated the earlier continuation pointers accordingly. [Progress register](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-6/05_arithmetic_gap_continuation/02_spatial_tensor_zero_spacings/research-progress/02_AGC_ST_ZERO_POSITIONS_RESEARCH_PROGRESS_20261120.md:7)
